The Story of Chanakya

I bow to Lord Jinendra, worshipped by the gods, and I write the story of Chanakya.

King Nand of Pataliputra (Patna) had three ministers — Kavi, Subandhu, and Shakatal. In the same city lived a priest named Kapil, whose wife was Devila. Chanakya was their son. He was very intelligent and learned in the Vedas.

Once, the neighbouring small kings joined forces and attacked Patna. Minister Kavi informed Nand of the attack. Nand, panicking, told the minister, "Go, somehow persuade those arrogant ones to retreat. Even if you have to give them money, do so." Following the king's order, the minister paid them off and sent them away. Truly, a kingdom cannot stand firm without a minister.

One day, Nand himself needed some money. He asked the treasurer how much was in the treasury. The treasurer replied, "Maharaj, the minister gave it all away to the enemies. Only a tiny amount remains." Although the king himself had ordered the money to be given, he could not see his own fault at that moment. Instead, instigated by others, he had the innocent minister and his entire family thrown into a blind well. The minister and his family suffered greatly there, given so little food and water that not even one person could properly fill their stomach. Truly, a king is no one's friend.

This injustice kindled the fire of revenge in Kavi's heart. The fire took a terrible form. Kavi told his family, "If we all share this meagre food, we shall slowly die one by one, and no one will be left to take revenge on the king for his cruelty. I cannot bear this. Therefore, let only the one among us who has the courage to take revenge eat this food." His family replied, "We see only you as capable of taking revenge. Therefore, we gladly say — you eat, and we shall all be satisfied."

Kavi ate the food, gathered his strength, and devised a plan. He managed to escape from the well and fled the city. He went to the forest, where he met a young Brahmin boy named Chanakya. Seeing the boy's intelligence and determination, Kavi recognised him as the instrument of his revenge. He trained Chanakya in all the arts of statecraft and warfare, instilling in him a burning desire to destroy King Nand.

Chanakya grew up to be a master strategist. He travelled from place to place, building alliances and gathering support. Eventually, he found a worthy ally in a young man named Chandragupta, who had the qualities of a true king. Chanakya trained Chandragupta and led him in a campaign against Nand. Through brilliant strategy and determined effort, they defeated Nand and destroyed his kingdom.

Chanakya then installed Chandragupta as the new king and became his chief minister. He ruled with wisdom and justice, ensuring that the kingdom prospered. He avenged his father Kavi's suffering and established a new dynasty that brought peace and prosperity to the land.

This story teaches that injustice sows the seeds of its own destruction. King Nand's cruel treatment of his innocent minister created an enemy who would ultimately bring about his downfall. And through the power of determination and wise counsel, even the most oppressed can rise to achieve great things. The wise should practise justice and compassion, for these are the foundations of lasting power.
